Short case 15 · General Surgery

Salivary Swelling

Three questions carry this case: is it the gland or a lymph node, is it benign or malignant, and is the facial nerve working? The last of those is free, takes ten seconds, and almost nobody does it before being asked.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The anatomy that makes the signs

Why the parotid has no true capsule, and why that matters
B&L: "The parotid, unlike other glands in the body, does not become encapsulated early to form a regular gland. The other structures in the vicinity, including the vessels, nerves and lymphatics, develop before encapsulation."​B&L 54 · p.831 That single embryological fact explains everything that follows: the facial nerve, the external carotid branches, the retromandibular vein and lymph nodes all end up inside the gland. So a parotid swelling may be a tumour of the gland or an intraparotid lymph node, and the nerve is in the way of both.
Superficial and deep "lobes"
B&L: "The facial nerve gets enveloped within the substance of the gland as it grows laterally, dividing the parotid gland into the superficial and deep lobes. Generally, the major functional component (80%) is superficial, whereas the deep lobe is usually the retromandibular component with minimal functional gland tissue."​B&L 54 · p.832 The "lobes" are therefore a surgical convenience defined by a nerve, not an anatomical division.
The landmark for finding the nerve
B&L: the retromandibular vein "generally lies deep to the facial nerve and is a constant landmark that is useful during the retrograde method of identification of the main trunk of the facial nerve".​B&L 54 · p.832 And the plane has a name: B&L calls it Patey's faciovenous plane.​B&L 54 · p.846
Where the nodes are
"Most of the lymph nodes lie in the superficial (preauricular) lobe of the parotid gland lateral to the masseter while very few lie in the deep (retromandibular) lobe."​B&L 54 · p.832
The ducts, for the stone question
The parotid or Stensen's duct passes over the masseter and enters the buccal mucosa through the buccinator at the level of the upper second molar tooth.​B&L 54 · p.832 SRB's etymology for the gland itself: para, around; otis, ear.​SRB 4 · p.392

2Examination

The curtain sign, with its mechanism SRB: a pleomorphic adenoma is a smooth, firm, lobulated, mobile swelling in front of the ear with a positive curtain sign, and the reason is anatomical: "As the deep fascia is attached above to the zygomatic bone, it acts as a curtain", so the swelling cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone.​SRB 4 · p.402

Two more signs from the same page: a raised ear lobule, and, where the deep lobe is involved, deviation of the uvula and pharyngeal wall towards the midline, plus restriction of jaw movements.​SRB 4 · p.402 So examine the mouth: SRB's figure is captioned "deep lobe tumour of parotid is examined per orally".​SRB 4 · p.402
1. Confirm it is the gland
A parotid swelling fills the hollow below and in front of the ear, lifts the ear lobule, and cannot be moved above the zygoma. Ask the patient to clench the teeth: the swelling becomes less distinct if it lies deep to masseter and more prominent if superficial to it.
2. Test the facial nerve, before you are asked
All five branches. A facial palsy with a parotid swelling means malignancy until proved otherwise, because a benign tumour displaces the nerve and a carcinoma invades it. It is the single most important examination finding in this case and it takes ten seconds.
3. Examine inside the mouth
For the duct orifice opposite the upper second molar, for pus or a stone, and for deep lobe extension pushing the tonsil and uvula medially.​SRB 4 · p.402 Bimanual palpation for the submandibular gland, with one finger inside the mouth and one outside, separates the gland from a lymph node.
4. Examine the neck nodes, and the other glands
Because a malignant salivary tumour metastasises to nodes, and because bilateral gland enlargement points to a systemic cause: Sjögren's syndrome, sialosis, or sarcoid.​SRB 4 · p.392
5. Look for skin fixity and pain
Pain, rapid growth, hard consistency, fixity to skin or deeper structures, nodes, and facial palsy are the features that mark a swelling as malignant.

3What it is likely to be

The proportions to quote
B&L: "Most salivary gland tumours (over 80%) occur in the major salivary glands and the majority of them are benign. Minor salivary gland tumours, in contrast, are more likely to be malignant (over 50%)." The commonest benign neoplasm is the pleomorphic adenoma, mostly in the parotid; the commonest malignant tumour is the mucoepidermoid carcinoma.​B&L 54 · p.838 SRB agrees: epithelial tumours are 90%, and mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignancy.​SRB 4 · p.400
The rule that followsThe smaller the gland, the likelier the malignancy. A swelling in a minor salivary gland of the palate is more than half likely to be cancer; one in the parotid is most likely benign.
Who gets what
B&L: "Warthin's tumours are more common in older men, while pleomorphic adenomas are slightly more common in women."​B&L 54 · p.838
Aetiology
Radiation exposure is implicated in both benign and malignant salivary tumours, and there is a strong association of smoking with Warthin's tumour. Also implicated: viral infections, environmental factors and industrial exposure including rubber manufacturing, nickel compounds and hair dyes.​B&L 54 · p.838
SRB's classification, with its figures
Adenomas: pleomorphic adenoma; monomorphic adenomas, that is adenolymphoma (Warthin's tumour), oncocytoma or oxyphil adenoma, seen in the elderly and in the parotid, and basal cell adenoma, which is rare. Carcinomas: mucoepidermoid, the commonest malignancy; acinic cell carcinoma, 1%; adenoid cystic carcinoma, very aggressive, 10%, common in minor salivary glands; adenocarcinoma; squamous cell carcinoma, 2%; carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma; and undifferentiated carcinoma.​SRB 4 · p.400
And the WHO classification, for the date
B&L: first classified by the WHO in 1972, with the last update in 2017.​B&L 54 · p.838

4Investigations

Ultrasound first, with guided sampling
B&L notes ultrasound is "invaluable for salivary gland pathology",​B&L 52 · p.780 and ultrasound-guided FNAC or core biopsy is the standard of care for determining the nature of a neck or glandular mass.​B&L 52 · p.781
What you must not do
Incisional or open biopsy of a parotid lump. B&L's reason, given of enucleation but applying to anything that breaches the capsule: it "may result in capsular breach and tumour spillage, increasing the possibility of local recurrence; it should be avoided".​B&L 54 · p.840 The tumour has pseudopods from its capsule, so spillage seeds the field.
For a stone
Plain radiograph, remembering B&L's figure: only 80% of stones are radio-opaque, so a normal film does not exclude one, and "in such cases, computed tomography scanning" or ultrasound is used.​B&L 54 · p.837 An occlusal view shows a submandibular stone.​B&L 54 · p.837
Cross-sectional imaging
For deep lobe extension, parapharyngeal spread, bone involvement and nodes; and CT of the thorax if malignancy is confirmed.​B&L 52 · p.780

5Treatment

Enucleation is condemned, so why does B&L endorse extracapsular dissection? SRB 4 p.403 and B&L 54 p.840 both condemn enucleation; B&L 54 p.846 and p.848 endorse extracapsular dissection as a different operation
Where the two books agree
SRB: "Enucleation is avoided as it causes high recurrence (50%) due to extension of tumour outside as pseudopods."​SRB 4 · p.403 B&L, of the same operation and for the same reason, the pseudopods from the tumour capsule: "Enucleation may result in capsular breach and tumour spillage, increasing the possibility of local recurrence; it should be avoided."​B&L 54 · p.840 No disagreement at all.
What B&L then endorses, which sounds like the same thing and is not
It lists extracapsular dissection first among the types of parotid surgery, from conservative to radical,​B&L 54 · p.846 and says: "Extracapsular tumour dissection does not require a formal facial nerve dissection; this reduces the incidence of temporary facial nerve palsy."​B&L 54 · p.846 And: "Extracapsular dissection for select benign parotid tumours is practised to avoid facial nerve dissection. It is reported to be as safe as parotidectomy." Technically, the fascia is incised in a cruciate or curvilinear manner to expose the tumour, and the tumour is dissected carefully in an extracapsular plane, visualising the facial nerve branches.​B&L 54 · p.848
These are two different operations with confusingly similar names, and the distinction is the answer.

Enucleation shells the tumour out of its capsule, so the capsule, and the pseudopods pushing through it, are left behind. Extracapsular dissection removes the tumour with its capsule and a thin cuff of surrounding gland, dissecting in the plane outside the capsule. One breaches the capsule; the other never opens it.

So answer: "Enucleation is condemned, because the tumour has pseudopods through its capsule, so shelling it out spills tumour and recurrence approaches 50%. Extracapsular dissection is a different operation: the tumour is removed with its capsule intact and a cuff of normal gland, which avoids a formal facial nerve dissection and is reported to be as safe as parotidectomy in selected benign tumours. For most pleomorphic adenomas in India the standard answer remains superficial parotidectomy, removing the parotid superficial to the facial nerve, with total conservative parotidectomy preserving the nerve if both lobes are involved."​SRB 4 · p.403​B&L 54 · p.846, p.848

Lead with superficial parotidectomy, because that is what your examiner expects, and offer extracapsular dissection as the modern alternative in selected cases. Never offer enucleation.
The operations, in B&L's order of increasing radicality
Extracapsular dissection · adequate parotidectomy · superficial parotidectomy · total conservative parotidectomy · radical parotidectomy.​B&L 54 · p.846 "Adequate parotidectomy involves removal of the tumour with a cuff of normal tissue in tail of parotid lesions, preserving function. It may not be possible to excise the tumour with a cuff of normal tissue in all the cases, especially when the lump is abutting the facial nerve."​B&L 54 · p.846
What decides which
B&L: presumed tumour histology; relation to the facial nerve plane, Patey's faciovenous plane; location of the tumour, particularly deep lobe; and facial nerve function.​B&L 54 · p.846 Those four, in that order, are the answer to "how would you plan the operation?"
SRB's version for a pleomorphic adenoma
Surgery is the first line treatment. If only the superficial lobe is involved, superficial parotidectomy, removing the parotid superficial to the facial nerve. If both lobes are involved, total conservative parotidectomy, retaining the facial nerve.​SRB 4 · p.403
If the nerve has to go
B&L: reconstruction using cable grafts from either the greater auricular nerve or the sural nerve.​B&L 54 · p.848
The closure detail that prevents a complication
B&L: separate the subcutaneous gland and overlying skin from the auriculotemporal nerve to avoid Frey's syndrome; place a suction drain anchored beneath the posterior belly of digastric and brought out posterior to the suture line.​B&L 54 · p.848
Frey's syndrome, explained properly B&L: the parotid's secretomotor supply travels with mixed sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres; this might contribute to "gustatory sweating", Frey syndrome, which involves sweating and flushing of the skin overlying the parotid region while eating in some patients following parotidectomy.​B&L 54 · p.833 The mechanism is aberrant regeneration: cut parasympathetic secretomotor fibres grow into the sweat glands of the overlying skin, so a stimulus that should make the gland secrete saliva makes the skin sweat instead. The preventive step is to interpose tissue between the auriculotemporal nerve and the skin flap.​B&L 54 · p.848

And the complication to warn about: "Temporary facial palsy is commonly seen in the lower branches."​B&L 54 · p.848
Salivary fistula, and SRB's elegant distinction SRB: incidence after parotid surgery is 0.2 to 3%, and there are two types.

Duct fistula, after superficial parotidectomy: profuse and often persisting. Management: ligate the duct with a non-absorbable suture as far anteriorly as possible, to allow normal saliva drainage from the deep lobe. If the common duct is ligated, the deep lobe atrophies without causing any fistula.​SRB 4 · p.399
Gland fistula, from the raw surface after superficial parotidectomy: mild, and settles within a month with anticholinergic drugs; Jacobson's tympanic neurectomy completely stops the secretion.​SRB 4 · p.399

Other causes: after drainage of a parotid abscess or a ruptured abscess, after biopsy, and trauma.​SRB 4 · p.399 Note that biopsy appears on that list, which is one more reason not to biopsy a parotid lump openly.

6Rapid-fire viva

Why are the facial nerve and lymph nodes inside the parotid gland?

Because of its embryology. Unlike other glands, the parotid does not become encapsulated early, and the surrounding structures, vessels, nerves and lymphatics, develop before encapsulation, so they end up enveloped within the gland.​B&L 54 · p.831 The facial nerve is enveloped as the gland grows laterally, dividing it into surgical superficial and deep lobes, with about 80% of the functional gland superficial and the deep lobe largely the retromandibular component with minimal gland tissue.​B&L 54 · p.832

What is the curtain sign, and why does it happen?

A parotid swelling cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone, because the deep fascia is attached above to the zygoma and acts as a curtain. It accompanies a smooth, firm, lobulated, mobile swelling in front of the ear, often with a raised ear lobule.​SRB 4 · p.402

How would you detect a deep lobe tumour?

Examine the mouth. Deep lobe involvement deviates the uvula and the pharyngeal wall towards the midline and may restrict jaw movements, and SRB's instruction is that the deep lobe tumour of the parotid is examined per orally.​SRB 4 · p.402 Confirm with cross-sectional imaging.

A parotid swelling with facial weakness. What does that mean?

Malignancy until proved otherwise, because a benign tumour displaces the facial nerve whereas a carcinoma invades it. Facial nerve function is one of the four things Bailey and Love says must be taken into account when planning the operation, alongside the presumed histology, the relation to Patey's faciovenous plane, and the location of the tumour.​B&L 54 · p.846 Test all five branches before you are asked.

Is a salivary swelling likely to be benign?

It depends which gland. Over 80% of salivary tumours occur in the major glands and the majority of those are benign; minor salivary gland tumours are more likely to be malignant, over 50%. The commonest benign tumour is the pleomorphic adenoma, mostly in the parotid, and the commonest malignancy is mucoepidermoid carcinoma.​B&L 54 · p.838​SRB 4 · p.400 So the smaller the gland, the likelier the malignancy.

Would you biopsy a parotid lump?

Not by open or incisional biopsy. Use ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology or core biopsy,​B&L 52 · p.781 because anything that breaches the capsule risks tumour spillage and local recurrence, the tumour having pseudopods through its capsule.​B&L 54 · p.840 Open biopsy also appears on SRB's list of causes of a salivary fistula.​SRB 4 · p.399

Why is enucleation condemned, and how is extracapsular dissection different?

Enucleation shells the tumour out of its capsule, leaving the capsule and the pseudopods pushing through it behind; SRB gives recurrence as 50%, and Bailey and Love says it may cause capsular breach and tumour spillage and should be avoided.​SRB 4 · p.403​B&L 54 · p.840 Extracapsular dissection is a different operation: the tumour is removed with its capsule intact and a cuff of normal gland, dissecting in the plane outside the capsule, which avoids a formal facial nerve dissection and reduces temporary facial palsy; it is reported to be as safe as parotidectomy in selected benign tumours.​B&L 54 · p.846, p.848 One breaches the capsule, the other never opens it.

What operation for a pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid?

Superficial parotidectomy if only the superficial lobe is involved, removing the parotid superficial to the facial nerve; total conservative parotidectomy retaining the facial nerve if both lobes are involved.​SRB 4 · p.403 Bailey and Love's spectrum runs extracapsular dissection, adequate parotidectomy, superficial parotidectomy, total conservative parotidectomy, radical parotidectomy,​B&L 54 · p.846 and the choice depends on presumed histology, the relation to the facial nerve plane, the location, and nerve function.

What is Frey's syndrome and how do you prevent it?

Gustatory sweating: sweating and flushing of the skin over the parotid region while eating, after parotidectomy, because the gland's secretomotor supply travels with mixed sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres.​B&L 54 · p.833 The mechanism is aberrant regeneration of cut parasympathetic secretomotor fibres into the sweat glands of the overlying skin. Prevent it by separating the subcutaneous gland and overlying skin from the auriculotemporal nerve at closure.​B&L 54 · p.848

Name the complications of parotidectomy.

Temporary facial palsy, commonly in the lower branches; permanent facial nerve injury, for which cable grafts from the greater auricular or sural nerve can be used; Frey's syndrome; salivary fistula; haematoma; and numbness.​B&L 54 · p.848 On the fistula, SRB gives an incidence of 0.2 to 3% and distinguishes a profuse, persistent duct fistula, managed by ligating the duct as far anteriorly as possible so the deep lobe still drains, from a mild gland fistula from the raw surface, which settles in a month with anticholinergics or can be stopped by Jacobson's tympanic neurectomy.​SRB 4 · p.399

Is a plain radiograph enough to exclude a salivary stone?

No: only 80% of stones are radio-opaque, so a stone can be missed, and in such cases CT or ultrasound is used.​B&L 54 · p.837 An occlusal view is the film for a submandibular stone.

Where does the parotid duct open?

Stensen's duct passes over the masseter and enters the buccal mucosa through the buccinator at the level of the upper second molar tooth.​B&L 54 · p.832 Inspect that orifice in every parotid case, for pus or a stone.

Which salivary tumour is associated with smoking, and in whom?

Warthin's tumour, that is adenolymphoma, which has a strong association with smoking and is more common in older men; pleomorphic adenoma is slightly more common in women.​B&L 54 · p.838 Radiation exposure is implicated in both benign and malignant salivary tumours, along with viral infections and industrial exposures including rubber manufacturing, nickel compounds and hair dyes.

Which salivary malignancy is the most aggressive, and where is it common?

SRB: adenoid cystic carcinoma, very aggressive, about 10%, and common in the minor salivary glands; mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the commonest malignancy overall, acinic cell carcinoma about 1%, and squamous cell carcinoma about 2%.​SRB 4 · p.400 Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notable for perineural spread, which is why margins are so difficult.

Bilateral parotid enlargement. What are you thinking?

A systemic cause rather than a tumour: Sjögren's syndrome, sialosis, sarcoidosis, and in the appropriate setting HIV-associated lymphoepithelial disease, mumps in an acute presentation, and parotid lymphoma. SRB's chapter covers Sjögren's syndrome, sialosis, sialectasis and parotid lymphoma alongside.​SRB 4 · p.392

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, disorders of the salivary glands are chapter 54. The two books agree on the main points, including condemning enucleation; the trap is the similarity of the names enucleation and extracapsular dissection, which are opposite operations, and the amber box above separates them.
